hook: Some city buses and racing cars store energy in a heavy spinning wheel: brake, and the wheel spins up; accelerate, and it hands the energy back. The wheel never goes anywhere, yet it holds a lot of energy. That is kinetic energy of turning, and it follows the same rule as a moving cart, with new letters.

figure.caption: Every piece of a spinning wheel moves, even though the center stays put, so the wheel has kinetic energy K = ½Iω².

chain.cause: A wheel turns at ω about a fixed axle
chain.effect: each piece of mass m at distance r moves at v = rω

chain.cause: Each piece has kinetic energy ½mv² = ½m r²ω²
Σmr² is the rotational inertia I
chain.effect: the wheel’s kinetic energy is K = ½Iω²

chain.cause: The same mass sits farther from the axle
chain.effect: I and so K are larger at the same ω

ideas: A turning object has rotational kinetic energy K = ½Iω², even if its center of mass is at rest.
It is the sum of ½mv² over every piece, with v = rω.
A scalar in joules; the direction of turning does not matter, because ω is squared.
K ∝ ω² at fixed I (doubling ω gives 4K) and K ∝ I at fixed ω.
K against ω² is a straight line with slope ½I.

misconception.wrong: A wheel spinning in place has no kinetic energy, because it is not going anywhere.
misconception.right: Every piece of the wheel is moving, so the wheel has kinetic energy ½Iω². Its momentum adds to zero because opposite sides move opposite ways, but kinetic energy is a scalar and does not cancel.

summary: An object turning about an axis has rotational kinetic energy K = ½Iω², the sum of ½mv² over all its pieces. It is a scalar in joules, is present even when the center of mass is at rest, grows with the square of ω and in proportion to the rotational inertia.
